title: She Had a Six-Figure Job in New York. H-1B Restrictions Made Leaving Easier.
excerpt: Data scientist Disha Lamba walked away from CVS Health and returned to India in May 2026, joining a growing number of Indian professionals choosing to leave the U.S. as visa policies tighten.
body:
• Disha Lamba, 28, left a data scientist role at CVS Health in New York and returned to India in May 2026, citing H-1B restrictions as a factor in her decision
  • Her departure comes as the Trump administration proposes a permanent $103,265 H-1B fee and moves to eliminate the 60-day grace period for laid-off visa holders
  • A Blind poll found nearly half of Indian professionals in the U.S. would consider returning to India if they lost their jobs
  • Canada's Express Entry and Global Talent Stream programs are attracting growing interest from Indian professionals weighing alternatives to the U.S.

Disha Lamba moved from India to New York University in 2021 at age 23, pursuing a master's degree in computer engineering. Five years later, with a six-figure data science job at CVS Health and an H-1B lottery selection in hand, she packed up and went home.

Lamba's decision to leave New York in May 2026 might seem counterintuitive — she had cleared what many Indian professionals spend years trying to achieve. CVS Health had sponsored her H-1B visa and informed her of her lottery selection in March 2026. But the restrictions that come with the visa, and the broader uncertainty facing Indian workers in the U.S., made walking away easier than staying.

"I felt like I was giving up a lot when I left the US," Lamba told Business Insider. She credited her time in New York with building her confidence, expanding her ambition, and shaping her career in machine learning and data science. At NYU, she attended conferences and meetups, where she connected with a senior CVS Health data scientist who encouraged her to apply. She landed the role in 2024.

But proximity to family and the weight of H-1B restrictions ultimately tipped the scale. She returned to India.

A Pattern, Not an Outlier

Lamba's story sits within a larger trend of Indian professionals reevaluating their futures in the United States. The calculus has shifted for many as the Trump administration has escalated restrictions on H-1B workers through 2025 and 2026.

The latest blow: the Department of Homeland Security completed its review on August 27 of a proposal to eliminate the discretionary 60-day grace period that H-1B and other visa holders receive after losing their jobs. The proposal, titled "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-day Grace Period," was listed as "Consistent with Change" after White House review. If finalized and published in the Federal Register, it would strip away the narrow window workers currently have to find new sponsorship, change status, or prepare to leave the country.

"Eliminating the 60-day grace period is both inhumane and unworkable. When a high-skilled worker faces a sudden termination, 60 days was already dangerously short. Stripping away this protection entirely leaves thousands of law-abiding individuals with zero time to wrap up their lives."

— Ajay Jain Bhutoria, former member, President's Advisory Commission on Asian Americans

That proposal arrives on the heels of DHS's proposed permanent $103,265 fee for all H-1B cap-subject petitions, published on August 25. The fee would apply on top of existing charges and cover both the regular 65,000-visa cap and the 20,000 slots reserved for U.S. master's degree holders — a category that many Indian graduates, including Lamba, fall into.

The Weight of Uncertainty

For those who remain, the pressures extend beyond fees and grace periods. Visa stamping appointments at U.S. consulates in India have been disrupted since mid-2025, with expanded social media vetting and a "Home Country Mandate" requiring biometric appointments and interviews exclusively in India. Cancellations and monthslong rescheduling have left workers stranded.

Meanwhile, layoff waves across Silicon Valley have intensified the stakes. More than 110,000 tech workers have lost jobs in 2026, according to Layoffs.fyi, with a significant portion believed to be H-1B holders. Meta's 8,000-job cut, Amazon's ongoing reductions, and LinkedIn's team trims have all contributed to what immigration attorneys describe as an unprecedented volume of requests for evidence and notices of intent to deny on change-of-status applications.

A poll on the anonymous professional network Blind found that nearly half of Indian professionals in the U.S. would consider returning to India if they lost their jobs — a figure that reflects both the practical limitations of the visa system and a shifting emotional calculus.

Alternative Destinations

Canada has emerged as a growing alternative. Its Express Entry system and Global Talent Stream programs have attracted increasing interest from Indian professionals who see a more predictable path to permanent residency. Some, like Microsoft technician Aishani B, who failed the H-1B lottery seven times before moving to Canada in 2022 and eventually securing a U.S. green card through the EB-1 extraordinary ability category in 2025, have found roundabout routes back.

India's own tech sector has also become a more viable landing spot. With the country's IT industry valued at $315 billion and venture capital flowing into startups across Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and the NCR region, returning professionals are finding opportunities that did not exist a decade ago.

What's Ahead

The 60-day grace period elimination still faces publication in the Federal Register and a public comment period before it can take effect. Nasscom, India's IT industry body, has said it is "actively engaged" with U.S. stakeholders over the proposed $103,265 fee. And a U.S. District Court in Boston struck down the original $100,000 fee in June, concluding it constituted an unlawful tax — a ruling that could shape legal challenges to the new proposal.

For Lamba and others like her, the question is no longer whether the American dream is worth pursuing. It is whether the terms of pursuit still make sense.
nri_angle: Indian professionals in the U.S. face mounting pressure from H-1B fee hikes, grace period elimination, and visa stamping delays, prompting some to leave for India or Canada.
author: Diaspora Desk
